full_judgment:
2. The petitioner is a Bangladeshi Private Limited Company represented by its Chief Executive Officer. In the course of business, the petitioner on 20-5-1996 signed an agreement with a public limited company under the name and style Wonderland Toys Ltd. to provide the required financial advisory/consultancy/ management services to the Wonderland Toys Ltd. for the purposes of their forthcoming public issue of shares to raise their capital on the basis of terms and conditions as embodied in the agreement. The Wonderland Toys Ltd filed an application dated 22-7-1996 supported by 13 other different documents including the aforesaid agreement to the Securities and Exchange Commission for approval of its prospectus for public offering of 500,000 ordinary shares of Taka 100 each. After considering the application and other documents including the agreement with the petitioner, the Securities and Exchange Commission by Memo dated 8-8-1996 (Annexure-C) approved the draft submitted by the said Wonderland Toys Ltd and permitted to publish the prospectus for public offering of shares, subscription opening on 19-8-1996 and closing on 26-8-1996. The Wonderland Toys Ltd after obtaining the consent of the Securities and Exchange Commission vide Securities and Exchange Commission letter dated 8-8-1996 and approval of prospectus affixed over the first page of proposed prospectus dated 8-8-1996, published their prospectus in the daily newspapers for public offering of shares, subscription of which opened on 19-8-1996 and closed on 26-8-1996. In the process of approval of prospectus all information including the financial statement, audited report of the Company and all other related papers were prepared by Wonderland Toys Ltd, its auditors and those others who were entrusted with the responsibility of preparation of particular papers. All such papers were submitted by Wonderland Toys Ltd. itself to the Securities and Exchange Commission and the petitioner had no role in preparing or submitting those papers. The petitioner had no knowledge as to the correctness of the contents of statements of those papers and also as to the correctness of information contained therein. The petitioner simply acted as per stipulations of their agreement dated 20-5-1996 with Wonderland Toys Ltd and the Securities and Exchange Commission was fully aware about the duties, obligations and responsibilities undertaken by the petitioner. 

 3. The Wonderland Toys Ltd published the prospectus in the National Dailies for public offering of shares and the petitioner as the company responsible for issue management of shares of Wonderland Toys Ltd discharged their duties in accordance with their agreement dated 20-5-1996 with Wonderland Toys Ltd and accordingly, their contractual obligations towards Wonderland Toys Ltd were fulfilled thereby treating the matter as closed. The petitioner's Chief Executive Officer, on receipt of an information of a friend found that the English Daily "Financial Express" in its 19th January, 2001 issue published news to the effect that Securities and Exchange Commissioner said to have held an enquiry purported to be an enquiry under section 21 of the Securities and Exchange Ordinance 1969 against Wonderland Toys Ltd as well as against the petitioner and based on that report, filed a criminal case against Wonderland Toys Ltd, its Directors and also implicated the petitioner. No notice of holding of any enquiry was ever served by Securities and Exchange Commission upon the petitioner and no enquiry was at all held by Securities and Exchange Commission as to business activities of petitioner, so far the issuance of initial public offering of shares of Wonderland Toys Ltd, is concerned for which the petitioner company was responsible for issue management of shares of Wonderland Toys Ltd, on the basis of the agreement dated 20-5-1996. The petitioner issued legal notice dated 15-2-2001 which was served on 18-2-2001 upon the respondent requesting him to supply within 72 hours of issuance of the legal notice, (i) a copy of so-called Enquiry Report, if any, as reported in the news item, to have been submitted by respondent's enquiry committee, upon holding enquiry against the petitioner at the back of it, under section 21 of Securities and Exchange Ordinance, 1969 and (ii) a copy of respondent's complaint petition, if any, as reported in the newspaper which has been filed before the Court of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) Dhaka. The respondent received the legal notice on 20-2-2001 affixing his seal in the Acknowledgment Card. As the respondent did not respond to the legal notice, the petitioner believes that the Securities and Exchange Commission has indeed, prepared a false Enquiry Report against the petitioner and its former Directors on the basis of imaginary and self-made enquiry. The non holding of enquiry by the respondent will also be clear from the fact that according to 19th January, 2001 issue of the English Daily "Financial Express", the respondent even implicated a former Director of the petitioner company, Shahjahan Kabir, a renowned banker and Founder Chairman of EXIM Bank Ltd, a private sector bank of the country, in their case, whereas Mr Kabir was on death bed in Singapore since January, 2000 and expired long ago on 31-5-2000 in Singapore. Section 21 of the Securities and Exchange Ordinance, 1969 does not envisage any provision for holding any enquiry about the business activities of a private limited company like the petitioner. 

 5. The petitioner also filed a Supplementary-Affidavit annexing the Enquiry Report dated 31-10-2000 which was marked as Annexure-H. It is stated that the respondent has actually ordered the Enquiry Committee to hold an enquiry under section 21 of the Securities and Exchange Ordinance, 1969 against Wonderland Toys Ltd vide his notification dated 27-6-2000 and in the subsequent extension of time the respondent had never mentioned anything in his letter of extension to hold any enquiry against the petitioner. The Enquiry Committee has gone beyond the scope of its terms of reference and all on a sudden at the end of the report under heading of Contraventions the Enquiry Committee most illegally entangled this petitioner without holding any enquiry against them about their business activities undertaken by them pursuant to the agreement. It is also stated that "the Enquiry Committee has observed that the company, i.e. Wonderland Toys Ltd, and the concerned Issue Manager, National Securities and Consultants Limited have contravened section 17(b)(c)(d) and (e) read with section 18 of the Securities and Exchange Ordinance 1969 in respect of issuance of its prospectus in August 1996." It is apparent from the Enquiry Report that neither there is any finding whatsoever at any place of the entire Enquiry Report against the petitioner nor there is any reference that the Enquiry Committee has been authorised by the respondent to hold any enquiry against the petitioner or that the said committee has notified the petitioner about holding of any enquiry against them about their business activities undertaken by them. The Enquiry Committee under the heading of "Contraventions" observed that the petitioner has contravened certain provisions of Regulations under the Securities and Exchange Commission (Merchant Banker and Portfolio Manager) Regulations, 1996 whereas the aforesaid regulation does not attract the petitioner as it was neither a Merchant Banker nor a Portfolio Manager, rather it acted as an independent company to provide the required financial advisory/consultancy/management services to the Wonderland Toys Ltd for the purpose of their forthcoming public issue of shares to raise their capital on the basis of terms and conditions as embodied in the Agreement and for that purpose the petitioner was called the 'Issue Manager'. 

 6. The respondent by filing Affidavit-in-Opposition contested the Rule denying the material allegations made in the writ petition and the Supplementary-Affidavit stating, inter alia, that the petitioner is, in fact seeking to have a specific criminal proceeding quashed invoking the writ jurisdiction for which there is other alternative and efficacious remedy under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and, as such, the writ petition is not maintainable. The writ petition involves disputed questions of facts resolution of which is not possible by affidavit and, as such, the writ petition is not maintainable. As per terms of the agreement between the Wonderland Toys Ltd. and the petitioner, preparation of prospectus as per regulatory requirements and filing for approval is the responsibility of the petitioner. The petitioner cannot avoid the responsibility of misstatement and suppression of material facts in the prospectus prepared by it. From the enquiry report it is clear that the petitioner either deliberately acted or failed to exercise its due diligence in discharging its duties as the issue manager which enabled the issuer company in resorting to undue and illegal practices of concealing material information in the prospectus with regard to the machinery, and thereby the petitioner contravened the provisions of Regulation 33(1)(Ka), (Ga), (Cha), (Chha) read with Regulation 35(1)(Ka) of the Securities and Exchange Commission (Merchant Banker and Portfolio Manager), Regulations 1996. 

 7. It is stated that no enquiry was ordered to be held against the petitioner and its involvement in the matter was revealed in the course of an enquiry in the matter of Wonderland Toys Ltd as connected facts. Secondly, the enquiry proceeding being a fact finding process does not require service of any prior notice either under the settled principle of law or under the provisions of section 21 of the Securities and Exchange Ordinance. The statements made in para 10 of the writ petition are product of misconception of law. In this regard, it is stated that the impugned enquiry was undertaken against Wonderland Toys Ltd. under the provisions of section 21 of the Securities and Exchange Ordinance, 1969 and in the course of such enquiry the petitioner's involvement in the matter was revealed as connected facts and accordingly, criminal proceeding has been initiated against the petitioner as per provisions of section 24 read with sections 17 and 18 of the Securities and Exchange Ordinance. The Securities and Exchange Commission has no legal obligation to explain its position to the petitioner. The grounds as enumerated in para-17 of the writ petition are untenable and misconceived and merit no consideration and, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged. The respondent also filed a Supplementary-Affidavit annexing the copy of the petition of complaint being Petition Case No.276 of 2001 against the writ petitioner and others which is still pending in the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka and the next date of the case was fixed on 26-4-2006 and a photocopy of the aforesaid, petition of complaint is marked as Annexure-I. 

 10. Mr Mahmudul Islam further submits that as per terms of agreement between Wonderland Toys Ltd and the petitioner, preparation of prospectus as per regulatory requirements and filing for approval is the responsibility of the petitioner and that the petitioner cannot avoid the responsibility of the misstatement and suppression of material facts in the prospectus prepared by it and from the enquiry report it is clear that the petitioner either deliberately acted or failed to exercise its due diligence in discharging its duties as the issue manager which enabled the issue company in resorting to undue and illegal practices of concealing material information in the prospectus with regard to the machinery, and thereby the petitioner contravened the provisions of Regulation 33(1)(Ka), (Ga), (Cha), (Chha) read with Regulation 35(1)(ka) of the Securities and Exchange Commission (Merchant Banker and Portfolio Manager) Regulations, 1996. He further submits that admittedly no enquiry was ordered to be held against the petitioner and its involvement in the matter was revealed in course of an enquiry in the matter of Wonderland Toys Ltd as connected facts and the inquiry proceeding being a fact finding process does not require service of any prior notice either under the settled principle of law or under the provisions of section 21 of the Securities and Exchange Ordinance and accordingly, criminal proceeding has been initiated against the petitioner as per provisions of section 24 read with sections 17 and 18 of the Securities and Exchange Ordinance and that the writ petition is the product of misconception of law and, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 12. Admittedly, the petitioner being a Bangladeshi Private Limited Company under the name and style "National Securities and Consultant Ltd" signed an agreement on 20-5-1996 with the public limited company, Wonderland Toys Limited, for rendering financial advisory/consultancy/management services to the Wonderland Toys Limited for the purposes of their forthcoming public issue of shares to raise their capital on the basis of terms, and conditions as embodied in the agreement dated 20-5-1996. The Wonderland Toys Limited filed an application on 22-7-1996 supported by 13 different documents including the aforesaid agreement dated 20-5-1996 to the Securities and Exchange Commission for approval of its prospectus for public offering of 500,000 ordinary shares of Taka 100 each. It is also admitted by the petitioner that the Securities and Exchange Commission vide Memo dated 8-8-1996 (Annexure-C) approved the draft prospectus submitted by Wonderland Toys Limited and permitted to publish the prospectus for public offering of shares, subscription opening on 19-8-1996 and closing on 26-8-1996. It is also the case of petitioner that Wonder land Toys Limited having obtained the approval of the Securities and Exchange Commission published the prospectus in the daily newspapers for public offering of shares. The petitioner has contended that in the process of approval of prospectus all information including the financial statement, audited report of the company and all other related papers were prepared by Wonderland Toys Limited, its Auditors and those others who were entrusted with the responsibility for preparation of particular papers, and all these were submitted by Wonderland Toys Limited to the Securities and Exchange Commission and the petitioner had no role in preparing or submitting those documents. Moreover, it is also the contention of the petitioner that they had no knowledge as to the correctness of the contents of the statements of those papers and also as to the correctness of information contained therein and the petitioner simply acted as per stipulations of their agreement dated 20-5-1996 with the Wonderland Toys Limited Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Advocate for the respondent, has drawn our attention to the agreement dated 20-5-1996 and submits that the range of service of the petitioner company will be amongst others as stated in Clause 2(a) of the Agreement, preparation of sanction of issue of capital as per regulatory requirements and filing for approval. 

 (a) Preparation of sanction of issue of capital as per regulatory requirements and filing for approval. 

 (c) Preparation of prospectus as per regulatory requirements and filing for approval. 

 14. On perusal of the Agreement dated 20-5-1996, it appears that according to the terms and conditions of the agreement between Wonderland Toys Limited and the petitioner, preparation of prospectus as per regulatory requirements and filing for approval is the responsibility of the petitioner, once the petitioner has undertaken the contractual obligation and responsibilities to provide the financial advisory, consultancy and management service for the purpose of Wonderland Toys Limited forthcoming public issue of shares to raise their capital through initial public offering and the petitioner company as per terms and agreement of the contract agreed to act as the manager to the issue, it cannot avoid the responsibility of misstatement or suppression of material facts in the prospectus prepared by it. In this context it is necessary to refer to the purpose intendment and the relevant provisions of the Securities and Exchange Ordinance, 1969, Securities and Exchange Commission Act, 1993 and the Rules and Regulations framed there-under. In the decision of the case of Shinepukur Holdings Ltd vs Security Exchange Commission reported in 50 DLR 291 at 294 parer-11 a Division Bench of this Court discussed the development of the concerned laws in the following terms: 

 19. Securities and Exchange Commission Public Issue Rules, 1998 has been framed under section 33 of the Security and Exchange Ordinance, 1969 for carrying out the purpose of the Ordinance. It is to be noted that the Securities and Exchange Commission Act, 1993 has been enacted for the purpose of establishment of a commission named the Securities and Exchange Commission for the protection of interests of the investors, development of the securities market and for the matters ancillary thereto. Section 5(1) of the Act, 1993 provides that the Commission shall consist of a chairman, four whole time members, an officer not below the rank of a Joint Secretary of the Ministry or Division of Finance to be nominated by that Ministry or Division. Sub-section (5) of section 5 provides that the Chairman shall be the chief executive of the commission. Section 25 empowers the Commission to make regulation with the approval of the Government for carrying out the purposes of the Act. The Securities and Exchange Commission (Merchant Banker and Portfolio Manager) Regulations, 1996 has been framed under section 25 of the Act, 1993. 

 20. Rule 3 of the Securities and Exchange Commission Public Issue Rules, 1998 enumerates the general requirements for filing an application by the issuer to the Securities and Exchange Commission for consent to an issue of capital which includes the submission of three copies of prospectus, together with all annexures signed by the concerned Officials. Rule 7 of the said Rules describes the format and contents of the prospectus which includes material information and information to be included in the prospectus According to Rule 7B, in the front cover page of the prospectus required information and some statements in bold type face be made, which provides that in giving the consent the Commission does not take any responsibility for the correctness of the statements made, the responsibility of which lies, amongst others, with the Issuer, Issue Manager and other personnel. Under Rule 14 of the Rules, 1998 the public company making initial public offering shall appoint an Issue Manager registered by the Securities and Exchange Commission, Rule 19 empowers Securities and Exchange Commission to impose penalty upon an issuer or its representative for violations of any of the provisions of the Rules, 1998 or for furnishing false or misleading information or suppression of any material information, as prescribed under the Securities and Exchange Ordinance 1969. Rule 20 of the Rules, 1998 enumerates a long list of documents which should be filed as exhibits to the application for consent to an issue of capital. Sub-Rule (6) of Rule 20 provides that if plant and machinery is reconditioned or second hand a certificate from SGS or Lloyds Agency on its economic life and price competitiveness duly certified by the Chamber of Commerce of the exporting country or country of origin be filed. According to Rule 20(10), due diligence certificate from the Issue Manager in original and Rule 20(13) Agreements with the Issue Manager and other officers be filed with the said application. In the instant case, from a careful scrutiny of the agreement dated 20-5-1996 between the Issuer, Wonderland Toys Limited and the Issue Manager, petitioner company and other materials on record it is abundantly clear that the petitioner company as the Issue Manager admittedly undertook the responsibility for preparation of prospectus as per regulatory requirements and filing for approval. In Para-6 of the writ petition the petitioner admitted that it has acted as per stipulations of their agreement dated 20-5-1996. When the petitioner has undertaken the responsibility to act as the manager to the issuer and render financial advisory, consultancy and management services to the Issuer, Wonderland Toys Limited, for preparation of their prospectus as per regulatory requirements for filing for approval to the Securities and Exchange Commission it cannot avoid the responsibility for the suppression of material facts. 

 21. According to section 2(g) of the Securities and Exchange Ordinance, 1969, Issuer means any person who has issued or proposes to issue any Security. The expression "Issue Manager" has neither been defined in the Ordinance of 1969 nor in the Act of 1993 nor in any of the Rules and Regulations framed there-under though the said expression has been used in the aforesaid Ordinance, Act. Rules and the Regulations. Issue Manager is an Officer of the Issuer and under section 2(h)(ii) of the Ordinance, 1969 'officer' in relation to an 'issuer' includes managing agents, manager secretary, accountant or auditor of the Issuer. In other words, an Issue Manager acts as the agent of the Issuer. Rule 14 of the Securities and Exchange Commission Public Issue Rules, 1998 enables the Public Company making initial public offering to appoint an Issue Manager registered by the Securities and Exchange Commission. One of the functions of a Merchant Banker is that of a Issue Manager as defined in Rule 2(Niyo) of the Securities and Exchange Commission (Merchant Banker and Portfolio Managers) Regulations, 1996 in the following terms: 

 22. According to Rule 2(c) of the Public Issue Rules 1998, merchant banker means any person who is engaged in the business of issue management, either by making arrangements regarding selling, buying, underwriting or subscribing to securities as underwriter, manager, consultant, adviser or rendering corporate advisory service in relation to such issue management. 

 23. In the instant case, agency relationship between the Issuer. Wonderland Toys Ltd and the Issue Manager, the National Securities and Consultant Ltd has arisen out of the Agreement dated 20-5-1996 and the statutory provisions of the aforesaid Laws, Rules and Regulations made thereunder. 

 25. The Appellate Division of the Supreme, Court of Bangladesh in the decision of the case of Chairman, Bangladesh Steel Mills vs Md Masood Reza reported in 30 DLR (SC) 169 held that it is, no doubt, the duty of an agent to conduct the business of his principal according to the direction given by the principal, but it is no part of his duty to carry out a direction which is not according to law. If the principal gives an order to his agent which is not lawful, the compliance with such an order amounts to an unlawful act which, according to the basic law of the society, he is not bound to do. Even if there is a contract or engagement between them that whatever order or direction will be given by the principal shall be obeyed unquestioningly, such a contract or engagement shall not be enforceable in a court of law, as it is void, so far as the unlawful order is concerned, being contrary to law and against the public policy. It appears that the instant writ petition involved disputed questions of facts which, according to our humble view, cannot be adjudicated in the writ jurisdiction. The respondent's case is that the petitioner either deliberately acted or failed to exercise its due diligence in discharging its duties as the Issue Manager which enabled the Issuer in resorting to undue illegal practice of concealing material information in the prospectus with regard to the machinery in contravention of the provisions of sections 17 and 18 of the Ordinance, 1969 and also violation of the Rule 20(6) of the Rules, 1998 in failing to submit required documents as exhibits to the Application for Consent to an Issue of Capital. Like the petitioner when the Issue Manager is the Merchant Banker its certificate of incorporation be cancelled for violation of its duties and obligations as per provisions of Regulation 33(1)(Ka), (Ga), (Cha) and (Chha) read with Regulation 35(1)(Ka) of the Securities and Exchange Commission (Merchant Banker and Portfolio Manager) Regulations 1996. Regulation 33 enumerates the grounds on which the Commission may cancel or suspend the certificate of the Merchant Banker or Portfolio Manager. Further, Regulation 35 describes the duties and obligations of the Merchant Banker or Portfolio Manager. 

 27. In the instant case, it appears that the respondent Securities and Exchange Commission held enquiry under section 21 against the affairs of the Issuer. Wonderland Toys Limited and in the course of such enquiry the petitioner's involvement (as Issue Manager) in the matter was revealed as connected facts and the enquiry proceeding being a fact finding process does not require service of any prior notice upon the Issue Manager-petitioner either in the settled principle of law or the provision of section 21 of the Ordinance. In the instant case, no enquiry was held against the affairs of the Issue Manager, petitioner rather the enquiry was held against the affairs of the Issuer, Wonderland Toys Limited and the petitioner's involvement in the matter was revealed as connected facts and the enquiry proceeding being a fact finding process does not require service of any prior notice either in the settled principle of law or under the provisions of section 21 of the Ordinance. In the case of Md Shamsul Islam Khan vs Secretary Ministry of Communication, Roads and Railways Division reported in 5 MLR (AD) 76 it has been held that holding preliminary enquiry in the nature of fact finding by a committee consisting of officers below the rank of the one involved in the matter under enquiry before the drawing up of the departmental proceeding is not-illegal. Because the preliminary enquiry in the nature of fact finding is not a part of the departmental proceeding in which officers senior to the involved officer be engaged as per provision of law. In the instant case, Criminal proceeding has been initiated against the Wonderland Toys Limited, the petitioner company and others under section 24 read with section 17 and 18 of the Securities and Exchange Ordinance, 1969. The provisions of section 21 is very clear which empower the Commission to hold an enquiry into the affairs of a Stock Exchange or any issuer of a listed security or the business as per section 21(1) of the Ordinance. It is the respondent who has categorically stated that no such enquiry was held against the petitioner and we also find from the Writ Petition and the Supplementary-Affidavit of the petitioner that no such enquiry was held against the petitioner. This being the admitted position, now the next question before us is to decide whether in the course of holding an enquiry against the Issurer to a listed security, the involvement of a company or Issue Manager, the Commission is competent to disclose such connected facts. In the facts and circumstances of the case we do not find any difficulty on the part of the respondent in disclosing such facts. In the instant case the petitioner admittedly agreed to act as the Manager to the issue and he also undertook amongst others to complete the preparation of prospectus as per regulatory requirements and filing for approval. But the alleged suppression of material facts by the petitioner said to have been revealed as the connected facts in the fact finding process. The Wonderland Toys Ltd alleged to have suppressed the material facts and the petitioner being the Manager to the Issue alleged to have failed to exercise due diligence in discharging their duties and thereby induced and influenced the issuer in resorting to undue or illegal practice of suppressing material facts and information in the prospectus with regard to the machinery in contravention of the relevant provisions of the aforesaid Ordinance of 1969, Regulations of 1996 and Rules of 1998 and obtained the consent of the Securities and Exchange Commission in publishing their prospectus in the daily newspaper for public offering of shares. 

 28. On perusal of Annexure-1 to the Supplementary-Affidavit submitted on behalf of the respondent, it appears that a criminal proceeding being Petition Case No.276 of 2001 corresponding to GR No. 77 of 2001 was initiated against the Wonderland Toys Limited, the petitioner and others as per provisions of section 24 read with section 17 of the Securities and Exchange Ordinance 1969. We do not find any illegality in holding an enquiry under section 21 of the Ordinance against the Wonderland Toys Limited and in the course of such enquiry the involvement of the petitioner was revealed as the connected facts and accordingly, criminal proceeding was also started against them. On perusal of the Enquiry Report and the petition of complaint it appears that the Enquiry Committee finds a prima facie case of contraventions of sections 17(b), (c), (d) and e(vi) read with section 18 of the Ordinance, 1969 in respect of issuance of its prospectus in August, 1996. It appears that the petitioner in order to avoid the due process of law before the trial Court under the Code of Criminal Procedure or to circumvent the equally efficacious alternative remedy under section 561A of the CrPC to quash the criminal proceedings pending before the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka filed the instant writ petition before this Court on misconception of law and obtained the instant Rule. In the decision of the case of Shinepukur Holdings Ltd vs Securities and Exchange Commission reported in 50 DLR (AD) 189 at page 192 Para-16 in reply to the petitioner's contention that "the report does not disclose any offence under section 17 of the Ordinance" the Appellate Division observed: 

 30. However, at the fag end of his submissions the learned Advocate for the petitioner has submitted that he does not press the second part of the Rule i.e. initiation of the criminal proceedings against them as reported in the English Daily Financial Express of 19th January, 2001. It appears that the respondent submitted a Supplementary-Affidavit annexing a true copy of the petition of complaint being Petition Case No. 276 of 2001 before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate. Dhaka which is marked as Annexure 1. It has also been submitted on behalf of the respondent that the order of stay obtained by the petitioner at the time of issuance of the Rule was subsequently vacated by order dated 20-8-2002. Having been confronted with such a situation the petitioner was advised not to press the second part of the Rule. Be that as it may, we have gone through the order dated 20-8-2002 passed by a Division Bench of this Court observing that since Regulation 35 enumerates the code of conduct of a Merchant Banker a complaint may be made against the petitioner for violation of the provisions of Regulation 35 of the Securities and Exchange Commission (Merchant Banker and Portfolio Manager) Regulations, 1996 read with section 17 of the Securities and Exchange Ordinance, 1969. The petitioner's contention is that the complaint case which has been filed against them is based on false allegations. Whether the allegation is true or false or whether the petitioner has any knowledge as to the correctness of the contents of statements contained in the financial statements, audited report of the company and other related papers or not or whether he failed to exercise due diligence or care and skill or not are disputed questions of fact. The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court in the decision of the case of Inland Fisheries Development Ltd vs Bangladesh reported in 5 MLR (AD) 71 held that disputed questions of fact cannot be decided in Writ jurisdiction. Accordingly, we are of the view that in the instant case these disputed questions of fact cannot be decided in Writ jurisdiction and the writ petition is not maintainable in law. As to the maintainability, at the fag end of the submissions, it has been asserted that the petitioner does not press the 2nd part of the Rule i.e. initiation of any criminal proceeding against them. Further, regarding the 2nd part of the Rule, the very basis of the petitioner's contention is that he has not violated the terms and conditions of the agreement dated 20-5-1996 and also has not violated any of the provisions of the regulatory requirements of law. At the present stage, it can be stated with certainty that whether the petitioner has violated any of the terms and conditions of the agreement or any provision of law or not is also a disputed question of fact which cannot be decided in Writ jurisdiction. 

 31. We have already observed that the petitioner has no reason to be aggrieved by the enquiry report because it is a preliminary enquiry in the nature of a fact finding process. We are of the considered view that on the basis of a fact finding process if the Commission of any offence is disclosed, the respondent authority is entitled to institute any criminal proceeding against the person or persons involved in the commission of the offence. In such a case before the initiation of the criminal proceeding the accused person is not legally entitled to get any opportunity of being heard and no show cause notice is required to be served upon said accused person. In the instant case, if the petitioner is aggrieved by the initiation of the criminal proceeding before the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka, then he will have enough opportunity to challenge the said proceeding under the Code of Criminal Procedure or to defend himself before that Court in accordance with law but he will not be entitled to invoke the Writ jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution in the guise of the breach of natural justice for quashment of the criminal proceedings pending in the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka.
